 EcoFlow has been a consistent top-performer in our tests, with one model earning the top spot in our guide to portable power stations. High-capacity, durable build, and reliable output are all strong with this line.
 So, the EcoFlow Delta 3 Classic with 45W solar panel for $479 (was $598) at Best Buy is an easy recommendation. If a power outage leaves you without heat controls, internet, or a working fridge, the Delta 3 Classic gives you a quiet, fume-free backup you can keep indoors.
 • Best for: Professionals, campers, and RV owners who want dependable backup power for outages or portable power on the go.
 • Why we like it: Beyond the strong performance in our tests, this EcoFlow model features 1,024Wh of long-life LFP battery capacity, 1,800W of continuous AC output to run big appliances, 3,000 charge cycles, and a five-year warranty. The solar panels for off-grid use sweeten this one considerably for us.
 • What you need to know: At $479 it’s good value for the battery alone, though the small panel is more of a bonus for added energy security rather than a serious charging option.
 Save $119
 Ecoflow Delta 3 Classic: was $598 now $479 at Best Buy A 1,024Wh portable power station with a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery rated for 3,000 cycles, 1,800W of continuous AC output with a 3,600W peak, and a weight of 26.7 pounds. This bundle includes a 45W solar panel and a protective bag, and it comes with a five-year warranty. EcoFlow sells and ships it through Best Buy’s marketplace.
 View Deal 
 Why We Recommend It
 EcoFlow is one of the biggest names in portable power, and the Delta 3 Classic is a pared-back version of its Delta 3 that keeps the essentials: a large, long-lasting LFP battery and enough output to run a full-size fridge or a space heater for a while. We haven’t tested this model ourselves, so this pick rests on EcoFlow’s track record and our experience testing other models. Expect fast charging, easy of use, and total dependability if you need additional or on-the-move power supply. The five-year warranty adds welcome peace of mind for a product you may rely on in an emergency.
 For more top picks, see our guide to the best portable power stations . 
 Price Context & Historical Value
 This is $119, or 20%, off the bundle’s $598 list price, which is a solid discount on a 1kWh power station with a five-year warranty. Keep in mind that the included 45W panel would take more than a full day of ideal sunlight to refill the battery, so think of it as a top-up tool rather than a full-blown charging solution. If you want backup power in place before winter, this is a good time to buy.
 Should you buy it?
 ✅ Buy the EcoFlow Delta 3 Classic bundle if... you want reliable backup power for outages, you need enough output to run a fridge, router, or CPAP machine, or you value a long-life LFP battery with a five-year warranty.
 ❌ Skip the EcoFlow Delta 3 Classic bundle if... you plan to rely on solar charging, since a 45W panel is far too small to refill this battery quickly, you need a power station that’s easy to carry long distances at 26.7 pounds, or you’d prefer to buy directly from Best Buy rather than a marketplace seller.

 The best laptop power banks are a must-buy when you're working away from a power socket. After all, even the best laptops for photo editing won't run on battery forever. And with governments telling us all to stock up on food and prepare for power outages, a power bank is a great way of ensuring you can keep vital devices going for a few days if the mains electricity fails to flow.
 But, the best iPhone power banks won't be powerful enough to do the job. Instead, you'll need a power bank with at least 18,000mAh capacity, as well as the right ports to connect to your specific laptop.
 As an added bonus, with a power bank this powerful, you'll be able to charge your cameras, tablets, phones,and other devices too. To find you the best model for your needs, we've put our experts to work. They've been testing and reviewing power banks, as well as using them within their own workflows, in order to compile this list of the absolute best.

With 1,024Wh of capacity and 2,200W continuous output (4,400W peak), it provides ample power for charging multiple drone batteries, cameras, and other essential gear on location. The two USB-C ports (140W each) allow for fast charging, while the SDC and SDC Lite ports support DJI’s proprietary adapters for even more efficient drone charging.
 Weighing 13kg, the Power 1000 is not the lightest option, but its sturdy build and rounded handles make it easy to carry. The clear display offers essential battery information, though it lacks smart features like an app or battery health monitoring. Additionally, there’s no built-in light or wireless charging, which could be a drawback for some users.

And knowing exactly how fast my laptop is charging is both just plain interesting to know, but I can also plan ahead to give make sure I have enough juice left throughout the day.
 The Anker Prime power isn’t just about a screen though, it also has a solid 20,000mAh of battery which I managed to get a few days' worth of keeping my phone and laptop going with short bursts of recharging, or one big recharge of my MacBook Pro 13. The big 200W maximum output, with a 100W single port output, also allowed me to use my laptop at full power. The power bank is a little boxy for slipping into pockets, but it looks great.

 FAQs 
 Will one of the best portable chargers work for a laptop?
 Sadly not, you will need a power bank with a much higher capacity than most power banks used to charge camera phones or other small appliances. It's recommended that you invest in a power bank with a 20,000 mAh or larger especially if you want to charge it multiple times. 
 How do I connect my laptop to the powerbank?
 How you connect your laptop to your power bank will depend on the time of charging cable your laptop needs. While most modern laptops such as the Apple Macbook Pro 14 M2 will have a USB C input, some older models might still use round AC adapters or a standard USB A input. For most homes that means about 2 kWh: our pick is the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2, which runs a typical fridge for about a day. The EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus is the pick if you want to start smaller and add a battery later, and the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 is the budget choice for short outages.
 We built this list from the makers’ own product pages, read on 17 October 2026. We have not run these units with a fridge ourselves, so the page is labeled as researched and the runtimes are our own sums from the published capacity. See how we research and rate products .
 How we worked out fridge runtimes
 A fridge’s motor runs on and off all day, so its average draw is much lower than the watts on its sticker. We used two example fridges:
 A fridge using 600 kWh a year (from its EnergyGuide label) averages about 70W, or about 1,640Wh a day.
 A fridge averaging 100W , for an older or larger model, uses about 2,400Wh a day.
 We then took 85% of each station’s capacity as usable, to allow for inverter losses, and divided by the fridge’s average watts. Your fridge may use more or less, so check its label or measure it.

 Most outages do not need the fridge to run nonstop. A full fridge that stays closed keeps food cold for a while without power, so some people run it for a few hours, unplug it, and plug it back in later. That stretches a 1 kWh battery much further, but it is your call how long your food can safely go; follow food-safety advice from your local health department.
 Solar also changes the sums. A unit that takes in more solar power than the fridge uses each day can keep going for as long as the sun shines. In our picks, the Anker F3800 Plus (3,200W), BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 (1,000W) and EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus (1,000W) take the most solar input; the Jackery units are limited to 400W.
 How to choose a portable power station for your refrigerator
 Find your fridge’s daily watt-hours. Look for the yearly kWh on the yellow EnergyGuide label or in the manual. Multiply by 1,000 and divide by 365. For example, 500 kWh a year is about 1,370Wh a day. Our guide on what size portable power station runs a refrigerator walks through the sums step by step, including a fridge plus a freezer.
 Pick the hours you need. Divide the station’s usable capacity (about 85% of its rating) by your fridge’s average watts. If you want the fridge running through a night and the next day, aim for about 2,000Wh. For a few hours, 1,000Wh is enough.
 Check the surge rating. A fridge draws a short burst of extra power when its compressor starts. Each pick here lists a surge or peak of 3,000W or more where the maker gives one; check your fridge’s manual if it has a starting-watts figure.
 Leave room for other essentials. Add the router, phone chargers and lights you will also run. For example, a 20W router and 40W of LED lights add 60W, or 1,440Wh over a full day.
 Think about recharging. If outages last more than a day, choose a unit with high solar input or expansion. See our list of the best portable power stations for home backup for more on sizing a whole setup.
 Who should skip a portable power station for a refrigerator
 If your outages regularly last several days and you have no solar panels, even a 2 kWh battery will run out on the first day. A larger system like the Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus with expansion batteries, or a fuel generator kept outdoors, will serve you better. And if you only need to keep a small dorm or mini fridge cold, a 1 kWh unit such as the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 is plenty; there is no need to pay for 2 kWh.
 Frequently asked questions about portable power stations for a refrigerator
 What size portable power station do I need to run a refrigerator? 
 For a typical full-size fridge, at least 1,000Wh for a few hours and about 2,000Wh to get through a night and the next day. Work it out from your fridge’s yearly kWh on its EnergyGuide label: divide by 365 for daily watt-hours, then add a 15% margin. A 600 kWh-a-year fridge uses about 1,640Wh a day.
 How long will a 1000W portable power station run a refrigerator? 
 It depends on the watt-hours, not the 1,000W output rating. A unit with about 1,000Wh runs a fridge averaging 70W for about 12 hours after losses. A unit with 2,000Wh runs it about twice as long.
 Can a portable power station run a refrigerator and freezer? 
 Yes, if its output covers both motors starting and its capacity covers both daily totals. Every pick here has at least 1,500W of continuous output. For both appliances through a long outage, a 2 kWh unit or larger is the safer size.
 How many watts does a refrigerator use? 
 Less on average than its label suggests. The watts on the label are what it draws while the compressor runs, but it cycles on and off, so its average draw is much lower. Use the yearly kWh figure on its EnergyGuide label, or measure it with a plug-in watt meter for 24 hours.
 Can I plug my refrigerator straight into a portable power station? 
 Yes. Plug the fridge’s cord into one of the station’s AC outlets. Use a heavy-duty cord if it needs to reach, and never connect the station to a wall outlet to power the house.
 Will a portable power station run a refrigerator during a power outage? 
 Yes. Any of the six picks here can run a standard household fridge from its AC outlets, because each puts out at least 1,500W continuously. How long it lasts depends on its watt-hours and your fridge’s average draw, from about 9 hours on a 1 kWh unit to about 46 hours on the 3,840Wh Anker F3800 Plus in our examples.

 How long will a portable power station run a refrigerator?
 About a day for most large units: 8 of the 10 we track lasted 20 hours or more. CNET ran

 Why doesn't a bigger battery always last longer?
 Because the power station uses power too. A fridge's compressor switches on and off, so for much of the test the
 station feeds a small load. Its inverter stays on the whole time, and that costs energy every hour.
 From CNET's figures we can split each battery's energy between the fridge and the station (7 units):
 The fridge used 54 W to 60 W on average in every one of those tests.
 The station itself used anything from 12 W ( Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 ) to 
 74 W (Oscal PowerMax 2400).
 Bigger isn't always longer. The Anker SOLIX F3000 has 
 50% more battery than the

 37.81% of its energy on itself, against 18.21%.
 Good capacity, poor fridge time. The Oscal PowerMax 2400 delivered 
 90% of its rated capacity in CNET's 480 W test. On the fridge, it spent more
 on itself than on the fridge.
 Our light-load data shows the same effect. 
 At a 34 W load, Outdoor Life got 49% to 71% of rated capacity from the 6 units we track that it tested. 
 At the heavier loads we count, the models we track deliver 75% to 96%. How we count tests 
 What size power station do I need for a refrigerator?
 Size it on usable capacity, not the number on the box. In CNET's test, 7 of the 8 models we
 track with a CNET capacity figure used 66 Wh to 91 Wh for each hour the fridge ran.
 The Oscal PowerMax 2400 used 134 Wh. For a fridge like CNET's, that
 means:
 Half a day (12 hours): about 800 Wh to 1,100 Wh usable.
 A full day (24 hours): about 1,600 Wh to 2,200 Wh usable.
 Two days (48 hours): about 3,200 Wh to 4,400 Wh usable.
 Usable capacity is what a unit delivers in independent tests. Every review page shows it, and the 
 real capacity table lists all of them. Your fridge may use more or less than CNET's, so
 the next section shows how to work it out.
 How do I work out the run time for my own fridge?
 Three steps, with a worked example:
 Find your fridge's average watts. Take the kWh per year from its yellow EnergyGuide label or its
 manual, and divide by 8.76. For example, 500 kWh a year ÷ 8.76 = 57 W.
 Add the station's own use. In CNET's test it ran from 12 W to 
 74 W. If you don't know a model's figure, the middle of CNET's results was about 31 W.
 Divide usable capacity by the total. The Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 has 1,812 Wh usable and
 uses about 12 W itself: 1,812 ÷ (57 + 12)
 = about 26.2 hours. On CNET's fridge, which used a little less, it ran for 27.40 hours.
 Real use often runs higher than the label, because door openings and a warm room add to it.
 Work it out in our run-time calculator : pick your power station,
 add your fridge's kWh a year, and add solar panels if you have them.
 Can a portable power station handle a fridge's start-up surge?
 Yes, at these sizes. A compressor draws a short burst of extra power each time it starts. All 19 units in
 CNET's test started and ran its fridge, which is rated at 7.2 A at 118 V (about 
 850 W at full load).
 Every model in our table is rated for at least 1,800 W of continuous output.
 For your own fridge, find its amps on the rating label or in the manual and multiply by 120 for a rough figure in
 watts. Keep that under the station's continuous rating. The label doesn't show the start-up burst, so leave room
 under the surge rating too. Every review page lists both ratings.
 Do I need a UPS mode to run a fridge?
 Not to run it, but it helps if the fridge stays plugged into the station. In UPS (pass-through) mode the fridge runs
 from the wall, and the station takes over when the power goes out. Nobody needs to be home to switch it.
 9 of the 10 models in our table list a UPS mode in their US manuals, with switchover times of 
 10 to 20 milliseconds.
 We couldn't check the Oscal PowerMax 2400.
 Each review page gives the switchover time and links to the manual.
 How long does food stay safe without power?
 Not long without a backup. 
 FoodSafety.gov

 Refrigerator: up to 4 hours, if you keep the door closed.
 Full freezer: about 48 hours, or 24 hours if it is half full.
 Every unit in CNET's test ran the fridge for at least 12.58 hours, more than 3 times

Best power station for a refrigerator

Written by

casey jenkins

in

Guides

Short answer first. For a standard full-size fridge, the sweet spot is the 2,000Wh class: in our sizing guide, 11 of the 20 stations in our database keep a typical fridge running a full 24 hours, and every one of them is 2,000Wh or larger. Our picks below come from those 11 — ranked by use case, not by commission. Prices are from manufacturer stores, checked October 2026, and they change; the check date is shown with each price.

Buying through affiliate links may earn us a commission.

Illustrative image — a generic station in a blackout scenario.
What a fridge actually draws

Three facts drive everything in this roundup (the full derivation is in our sizing guide for refrigerators):

Running watts are modest. A typical full-size fridge’s compressor draws about 150W while it runs.
It doesn’t run constantly. The compressor cycles on and off — a duty cycle of roughly 35% is the standard planning figure. That puts daily consumption at about 1,260Wh (150W × 24h × 35%).
Startup surge is brief but real. When the compressor kicks on, it can spike to roughly 750–1,200W for a fraction of a second (Estimate). Every station below clears that spike on continuous output alone — for a fridge, capacity runs out long before power does.

Apply our standard planning math — required capacity = energy ÷ 0.85 inverter efficiency × 1.20 reserve — and a full 24 hours needs about 1,779Wh of rated capacity. All runtimes below are Estimates at 80–90% inverter efficiency, assuming the fridge above.

The picks
Best overall — EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max
Capacity: 2,048Wh · Est. fridge runtime: 31–35 hrs · Price: $899 (checked Oct 15, 2026)
2,400W continuous / 4,800W surge (Manufacturer specification); 44.8 lbs

The DELTA 3 Max does the full day with roughly a third of its battery to spare, and it’s the easiest of the full-day stations to live with: at 44.8 lbs it’s near the light end of the class, and it recharges from a wall outlet faster than anything else here — 0–80% in about 68 minutes, which matters when the grid flickers back for an hour mid-outage.

Limitation: it’s a fixed size. The base DELTA 3 Max has no extra-battery port (expansion is a feature of the separate DELTA 3 Max Plus), and its 500W solar input ceiling is modest for its size — fine for topping up, slow for multi-day solar-only running.

Choose this if — you want a full day or more of fridge runtime (31–35 hours) at the lowest price in the 2,000Wh class.

Spend more only if — you need expansion batteries or multi-day cover; that step up is the DELTA Pro 3.

Main limitation — the base unit is not expandable, and solar input is capped at 500W.

Check price at Amazon
Best budget — BLUETTI Elite 200 V2
Capacity: 2,073.6Wh · Est. fridge runtime: 32–36 hrs · Price: $899 (checked Oct 15, 2026)
2,600W continuous / 3,900W surge (Manufacturer specification); 53.4 lbs

Two stations in this roundup wear a $899 tag; the Elite 200 V2 returns the most fridge-hours for it. It holds the most capacity of the three, posts the longest estimated runtime in the 2,000Wh class, and works out to about $434 per kWh — the lowest cost per unit of storage of all 11 full-day matches. Its 2,600W continuous output is also the highest in the class, and BLUETTI rates the battery for 6,000+ cycles.

Limitation: at 53.4 lbs it’s the heaviest of the $899 stations — roughly 9 lbs more than the DELTA 3 Max for about an extra hour of runtime. Like the DELTA 3 Max, it isn’t expandable.

Choose this if — you want the most capacity in the class (2,073.6Wh) and BLUETTI’s 5-year warranty at the same $899.

Spend more only if — you need to expand later or run bigger loads; that means the DELTA Pro 3 class.

Main limitation — at 53.4 lbs it is the heaviest pick here, and it is not expandable.

Check price at BLUETTI
Best for long outages — EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3
Capacity: 4,096Wh · Est. fridge runtime: 62–70 hrs · Price: $2,799 (checked Oct 15, 2026)
4,000W continuous / 8,000W surge (Manufacturer specification); 113.5 lbs; expandable to 12,288Wh

If your outages run two or three days, this is the pick. On its own it carries our example fridge for roughly two and a half days; add up to two extra batteries and the same fridge runs past five days (Estimate). It also takes up to 2,600W of solar — the most here — so a sunny day genuinely refills it, and EcoFlow lists it as UL 9540 certified. (The Anker SOLIX F3800 in the table below is the alternative if you want even more expansion headroom — up to 26,880Wh — at a lower starting price.)

Limitation: 113.5 lbs on wheels. This is a unit you park next to the fridge before the storm, not one you carry room to room. And at $2,799, you’re paying for whole-home output (including 240V) that a fridge alone will never use.

Choose this if — your outages run several days, or you want the option to expand up to 12kWh later.

Spend more only if — you do not need to; this is the step-up pick, and it only earns its price when multi-day cover is a real scenario.

Main limitation — $2,799 is about three times the Best overall pick, for runtime most one-day outages never use.

Check price at Amazon
Best compact — Jackery Explorer 2000 v2
Capacity: 2,042Wh · Est. fridge runtime: 31–35 hrs · Price: $999 (checked Nov 2, 2026)
2,200W continuous / 4,400W surge (Manufacturer specification); 39.4 lbs

The Explorer 2000 v2 is the lightest station that makes the full 24 hours — 39.4 lbs, about 14 lbs less than the Elite 200 V2 and the easiest here to carry up stairs or load into a car. It gives up nothing on the core job: the same 31–35-hour estimated fridge runtime as the rest of the 2,000Wh class, with five AC outlets.

Limitation: no expansion port, and its 400W solar input ceiling is the lowest in this roundup — irrelevant for a one-day outage, a real constraint if you later want to stretch into multi-day solar running. Its fastest recharge (~1.7 hours) also requires turning on emergency charging in the Jackery app.

Choose this if — you will move the station often; at 39.4 lbs it is the lightest in the class.

Spend more only if — you need expansion or heavier loads; see the DELTA Pro 3.

Main limitation — at $999 it costs $100 more than the DELTA 3 Max for the same fridge runtime.

Two honest notes on the table. The Explorer 3000 Pro’s $2,499 is Jackery’s refurbished price — it’s no longer sold new in the US — and it’s the worst value per kWh here. The F2000 matches the 2,000Wh class on runtime but costs more than double the $899 stations; it’s in the table because it’s a verified full match, not because we’d send you to it first.

What didn’t make the cut: the entire 1,000Wh class. Good stations — the BLUETTI AC180 ($449) runs our example fridge an estimated 18–20 hours — but none of them reaches 24 hours. If your outages are almost always under ~18 hours, that class saves real money; just buy it knowing where the wall is.

How to choose

Start with your fridge, not our example. Your EnergyGuide label (annual kWh × 1,000 ÷ 365) gives your fridge’s real daily use in watt-hours. Our sizing article walks through substituting it into the same formula. Runtimes here are calculated estimates at 85% inverter efficiency, run to empty; the 20% reserve is built into the capacities we recommend, not subtracted from the hours shown.

Respect the duty cycle. The 35% figure assumes a reasonably cool room and a closed door. A fridge in a hot garage, opened often, can hit a 50% duty cycle — daily need climbs to roughly 2,540Wh, the 2,000Wh class falls short, and the 3,600Wh tier becomes the honest answer.

The runtime headroom is your second-load budget. Every 2,000Wh pick above runs the fridge 31–36 hours, not 24 — that surplus is what powers a router, lights, and phone charging alongside it. Add a freezer or a work-from-home setup and the surplus disappears fast; that’s what the calculator is for.

Buy expansion only if you’ll use it. Among the picks, only the DELTA Pro 3 grows after purchase. If your outages are reliably one day, a fixed 2,000Wh station at $899 beats a $2,799 expandable one you never expand.

Your next step

Run your own fridge — and everything you want alongside it — through the Outage Brief sizing guide. The fridge preset uses the same duty-cycle, efficiency, and reserve math as this article, applied to all 20 stations in our database.

And before you buy, check the Verified Deals page — we re-check the prices there every week.

Brands define those figures differently: Jackery lists 50W of standby consumption for the 5000 Plus, BLUETTI as low as 4W of idle draw for the FridgePower and Anker 6W of active idle power for the S2000. EcoFlow lists no figure for the DELTA Pro, and our comparison data holds none for the DELTA 3 Max.
 How much power does your refrigerator use?
 Start with the yellow EnergyGuide label . Its yearly kWh is an estimate from a standardized test, not a measurement in your kitchen. Here is a label of 700kWh a year, step by step:
 Energy a day: 700kWh ÷ 365 = about 1.92kWh. × 1,000 = about 1,918Wh a day.
 With our 20% allowance: 1,918Wh × 1.2 = about 2,301Wh load budget, and 2,301Wh ÷ 0.85 gives a calculated reference size of 2,708Wh rated under our assumptions.
 Before the allowance: 1,918Wh ÷ 0.85 gives 2,257Wh rated.
 Average power, a separate figure: 700 × 1,000 ÷ 8,760 hours = about 80W around the clock.
 Calculations use unrounded values, so a step done with the rounded figures shown can differ by 1Wh. 
 Calculations use the unrounded values, and displayed figures are rounded. Capacities are rounded up. The 0.85 is our planning share of rated capacity that reaches AC devices, not a measured inverter efficiency.
 The plate inside the fridge often lists amps. That number is not the running draw, because on frost-free models it can include the defrost heater. Volts × amps from the plate gives VA, not published watts. A plug-in energy meter left on for a few days, where your fridge’s manual allows one, records the use of your fridge in your kitchen. Our refrigerator watts guide and refrigerator amps guide go through both.

 Will a power station start your fridge?
 Running watts and start-up load are two separate numbers. A station that handles your fridge’s running watts can still fail its start, so check the surge separately. For a moment at start-up, the compressor pulls more than its running power. GE Appliances puts that surge at about twice the running power, for a second or two.
 Generator wattage charts give starting figures, but they do not all mean the same thing. Champion’s wattage flyer lists a refrigerator at 400 running watts and 2,200 starting watts. It defines starting watts as the extra power some devices need to turn on, and its method adds them to the running watts. So that fridge’s total start-up load on Champion’s figures is about 2,600W (400W + 2,200W). Honda lists 1,600W starting wattage for a refrigerator, and Champion’s current chart lists 800 to 1,200W. Neither chart says whether its figure is the total or the extra.
 We use a listed surge of 2,600W as an editorial screening threshold. It is not a compatibility standard. The surge column on this page is the maker’s listed AC surge or peak output, the total the station’s inverter can deliver for a moment. It is not the extra watts above the running load. Overload modes that lower the voltage to run heaters, such as BLUETTI’s Power Lifting mode and EcoFlow’s reduced-voltage overload mode, do not count as surge.
 A listed surge rating is a maker claim, not a test with your fridge. The best check is to plug the fridge into the station while the grid is on and let it run through a few compressor starts. Start nothing else large, such as a microwave, at the same moment, as Honda advises for generators.
 A fridge and a freezer on one battery
 Our example day: a fridge at 250W for 40% of the time (2,400Wh) and a chest freezer at 1,000Wh a day, the top of the range in our chest freezer guide . That is 3,400Wh, an average of about 141.7W. With our 20% allowance it gives a calculated reference size of 4,800Wh rated under our assumptions (3,400Wh × 1.2 ÷ 0.85). Before the allowance the figure is 4,000Wh (3,400Wh ÷ 0.85). If both appliances use less than our example, a smaller system may be sufficient. Calculate from their combined energy use and check startup compatibility separately.
 For this job we screen at a listed surge of 3,000W. It is an editorial threshold set above our 2,600W fridge figure, not a calculated start of both compressors at once. Our chest freezer guide uses about 800W for a freezer start, and the source does not say whether that is total or extra. If both compressors could start at the same moment, the load could go above 3,000W. This is an example, not a compatibility test. Passing this filter does not establish that both compressors can start together. Check the relevant output limits and the appliances’ actual startup requirements separately.

 FoodSafety.gov gives approximate times, not exact safe limits. A full freezer that started frozen and stays closed may hold a safe temperature for about 48 hours, and a half-full one for about 24. A closed fridge keeps food safe for up to about 4 hours. For what to keep and what to throw out after an outage, use the FoodSafety.gov power outage food safety chart . Our suggestion: if the battery cannot run both, give the fridge the battery and keep the freezer closed and full. Our guide on how long a fridge can go without power covers the food side.
 When nobody is home: a checklist
 A station on a shelf does nothing until someone plugs the fridge into it. For an outage while you are at work or away, the station has to stay between the wall and the fridge and switch over by itself. We do not pick a winner for this job. Check these points in the manual of the model you choose, and test what you can while the grid is on:
 Automatic switchover. The time is the maker’s figure for the station’s outlets while it stays plugged into the grid, not a test with your fridge.
 Output auto-off. Some stations turn off an AC output after a period of low draw. Check whether that can trigger while the fridge compressor is off between cycles, and whether you can turn it off.
 Settings after a restart. Check whether the UPS mode, AC output and other settings stay on after the station restarts.
 Full depletion and the grid’s return. Check what the station does when the battery runs empty, and whether it restarts the AC output and recharges on its own when the power comes back.
 Pass-through limits. Check whether pass-through mode has its own current or output limit, separate from the battery output.
 Your fridge’s restart. With the fridge running on the station, unplug the station from the wall and confirm that the fridge keeps running or starts again on its own.
 An app that reports over the internet stops reporting if the outage takes down your router or internet service. An appliance thermometer shows the temperature when you read it. To establish what happened while you were away, use a device that records temperature history. A cold reading after power returns does not prove that the food remained cold throughout the outage.
 What not to do
 Do not feed the fridge circuit through a wall outlet. Plugging a station or generator into an outlet to power house wiring is backfeeding, which the CPSC warns can electrocute utility workers. For house circuits, a licensed electrician installs a transfer switch or an inlet with an interlock. Without one, plug only the fridge’s own cord into the station.
 Do not run a gas generator indoors to recharge it. The CPSC says to run generators outside, at least 20 feet from the house, with the exhaust pointed away from it.
 No extension cord or adapter between the station and the fridge. This is our suggestion, based on GE’s refrigerator manual , which says not to use an extension cord or an adapter with the fridge. Check your own fridge’s manual, and put the station next to the fridge.
 Other models we considered
 Anker SOLIX S2000 : 2,010Wh and a 3,000W surge, last checked at $729.99 with coupon on November 2. On October 28, 2026, Anker's US store said that orders placed on or after October 5 ship within 10 to 15 business days. Under our rule that is not in stock, so it does not rank until the store ships it without a stated wait.
 Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus : meets our full-day threshold at 3,584Wh. It loses the full-day pick to the DELTA Pro on price, or on rated capacity when the two prices tie. If its price drops below the DELTA Pro, it takes the full-day pick.
 EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 : a calculated near-one-day example before allowance. At 4,096Wh its illustrative runtime on our 3,400Wh fridge and freezer day is about 24.6 hours with no allowance, and it stays under the 4,800Wh our allowance gives. It costs $700 less than the Explorer 5000 Plus.
 BLUETTI FridgePower : built to sit between the wall and a fridge. BLUETTI lists a switchover of 10 ms or less, and it is 3.07 inches thick with its feet, so it mounts on a wall or sits on the fridge top. Three BlueCell 200 batteries raise it to 8,064Wh in total (2,016Wh × 4). It has two AC outlets and no USB ports. It loses the night pick to the DELTA 3 Max on price, or on rated capacity when the two prices tie, 2,016Wh against 2,048Wh. Reviewed (June 15, 2026) ran a full-size fridge for more than 30 hours with the door closed. In APH Networks' test (April 24, 2026), two hair dryers tripped it at a 2,896W spike, below the 3,600W surge BLUETTI lists. That load is not a fridge compressor, so the result neither confirms nor rules out a start with your fridge.
 Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 : passes the start-up filter with a 4,000W surge and holds 2,048Wh, for $121 more than the DELTA 3 Max. Anker lists expansion up to 4kWh in total.
 BLUETTI AC200L : 2,048Wh, 3,600W surge and growth to 8,192Wh in total, at 62.4 lb. On October 28, 2026 its product page at BLUETTI's US store showed no buy button, so we could not confirm that it is in stock. It does not rank until a new check.
 BLUETTI Elite 300 : Surge figure not counted: BLUETTI lists 4,800W as both surge and lifting power. At 3,014Wh it is also under our 3,389Wh full-day threshold.
 BLUETTI Apex 300 , Elite 200 V2 and Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus : Verified surge specification not yet recorded in our comparison data. No surge figure located in the documents we reviewed, the US product pages and US user manuals or guides checked on October 28, 2026.
 EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra : the largest base capacity among the eligible models we track, 6,144Wh, about 52.2 hours of illustrative runtime at a 100W average (6,144Wh × 0.85 ÷ 100W). It meets the fridge and freezer threshold but costs $700 more than the Explorer 5000 Plus.
 Anker SOLIX F3800 : its store price was last confirmed more than 72 hours ago, so it does not rank until a new check.
 These models did not win under our rules for this page. Some fit other jobs, as their reviews explain.
 How we chose these picks
 We compared the 32 portable power stations in the PowerSized database, US versions only. It is the list of models we track, not every station sold in the US. A model is eligible when the configuration we price is in stock at the brand’s US store, its price was checked in the last 72 hours and its PowerSized review is published, so our recommendation pool is narrower than the database. In stock means the configuration can be ordered and ships without a stated future date or a stated wait longer than about a week. A pre-order or a backorder does not count. Then:

 a rated capacity of at least 3,389Wh (100W × 24 h × 1.2 ÷ 0.85), then the lowest current price 
 Fridge and freezer for a day

 Price tie

 Each threshold includes our 20% allowance on the load’s energy, and capacities are rounded up. They are scenarios for choosing, not guaranteed minimum sizes. We count 85% of rated capacity as reaching AC devices, our planning share, not a measured inverter efficiency. Prices are for the base unit as the store sells it, without panels or extra batteries. A member price counts and is labeled. Runtimes are our calculations, not tests with a fridge. A surge counts only when the maker publishes it as AC surge or peak output in US material we can show. The full method is on How we rate , and the buying basics are in what to look for in a portable power station .
 Questions buyers ask
 Is there a power station that will run a refrigerator? Many can, if the station's surge rating handles your fridge's start and its capacity holds the hours you need. All three picks above list a surge of 4,800W or more, but a listed surge is not a test with your fridge. By our calculation, the 2,048Wh DELTA 3 Max has an illustrative runtime of about 17.4 hours with a fridge that averages 100W (2,048Wh × 0.85 ÷ 100W), before any allowance. Plug your fridge in and let it start a few times while the grid is on before you rely on it.
 What size battery backup do I need for a refrigerator? Rated Wh = yearly kWh on the EnergyGuide label × 1,000 ÷ 365 × the days you want × 1.2 ÷ 0.85. A 700kWh label gives a calculated reference size of 2,708Wh rated for one day under our assumptions, with our 20% allowance. With our 100W planning scenario, one day gives 3,389Wh. These are reference sizes from our assumptions, not validated minimums for your fridge. Check the surge rating separately.
 What size solar generator runs a refrigerator and a freezer? On our example figures, a full day of both gives a calculated reference size of 4,800Wh rated under our assumptions, with our 20% allowance (3,400Wh × 1.2 ÷ 0.85). We also screen for a listed surge of 3,000W or more. If both appliances use less than our example, a smaller system may be sufficient. Solar then recharges it. How fast depends on the panels, the sun and the station's solar input. Our solar generator picks compare kits.
 Can I use a battery generator for a fridge indoors? A battery power station has no combustion exhaust, but fans and inverter noise vary. Keep it on a hard, dry surface with its vents clear and follow its manual. A gas generator is different: the CPSC says to run it outside, at least 20 feet from the house, with the exhaust pointed away from it.
 Can I use an extension cord between the station and the fridge? GE's refrigerator manual says not to use an extension cord or an adapter with the fridge. Our suggestion is to put the station next to the fridge instead. For a gas generator outdoors, follow the generator maker's guidance on cord rating and length.
 Can a battery backup work like a UPS for a refrigerator? Many list an automatic switchover. The station stays between the wall and the fridge and moves to its battery when the power drops. Each of our three picks lists a switchover of under 30 ms, the maker's figure for the station while it stays plugged into the grid, and Jackery lists 0 ms for the Explorer 5000 Plus in Online UPS mode. The figure for each pick is in the ports table above. We do not rank models for this job. Check output auto-off, restart behavior and pass-through limits in the manual, and confirm that your fridge starts again on its own. Our checklist lists each point.
 Is Jackery or EcoFlow better for a refrigerator? Neither brand wins every job in our data. Our picks follow the price, stock and capacity rules above, so the brand of a pick can change after a new price check. Warranty and support differ by brand, and our brand comparison lists them.

 About 12 h for a generic 1,000 Wh unit, if its inverter can handle the 1,000 W startup surge: roughly 800 Wh (80% of rated) reaches the outlets, divided by an average draw of 67 W. Measured models of this size vary; see the table above.
 Which power station can run a refrigerator for a full day?
 Of the 34 current models we track, the smallest that runs a refrigerator for 24 hours on one charge is the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2. Larger models run it longer; see the table above.
